Dilnaz: hey, you okay? you've been quiet at work
Gopika: fine
Dilnaz: you said "fine" in the team chat three times today 🙂
Gopika: I've just got a lot on
Dilnaz: I know. You've covered Tuesday, Thursday, plus Ruchi's report, plus the party plan
Gopika: someone has to
Dilnaz: Not always you though. Can I take the Friday report off you? I'd like to
Gopika: you don't have to
Dilnaz: I want to. Also I'm bringing you dinner tonight, no discussion 😊
Gopika: ...ok
Gopika: thank you. I didn't realise how tired I was 🥺

qa.q: What did Dilnaz offer to take off Gopika's plate?
qa.a: Dilnaz offered to take the Friday report.

qa.q: What was Dilnaz noticing and feeling about Gopika's replies?
qa.a: Dilnaz was concerned, noticing short answers such as "fine" three times and the growing list of work Gopika was covering.

qa.q: What kind of help did Dilnaz offer that made it easy for Gopika to accept?
qa.a: Dilnaz offered something specific, the Friday report, and dinner that night, saying no discussion was needed. It was concrete and kind.

qa.q: How might Gopika have felt at first when Dilnaz asked whether Gopika was okay?
qa.a: Gopika likely felt guarded and reluctant to admit being tired, as the short "fine" and "someone has to" suggest. Later Gopika admitted the tiredness. 🤍

passage:
At the tea stall near the bus stand, Tenzin noticed the shutters of the women's sewing group were down again. Ayesha, who ran it, had mended half the village's school bags and lent money and advice to everyone. Lately she answered in one word, and the last two times he greeted her, she passed without looking up.
That afternoon he walked to her house with a flask and two glasses. "You've done so much for us all," he said, standing at the gate. "I thought it was my turn."
Ayesha stared at the flask. "I'm just tired, Tenzin," she said. Her voice cracked.
"I'll sit at the sewing room tomorrow and hand out the bags," he said. "You rest."
She poured the tea. It was the first time in weeks she had let someone else.

qa.q: What did Tenzin bring when he visited Ayesha's house?
qa.a: He brought a flask and two glasses.

qa.q: What was Tenzin worried about as Ayesha passed him without looking up?
qa.a: Tenzin was worried, having noticed the change from her usual warmth, and felt it was time to give back to someone who had given so much.

qa.q: What made Tenzin's offer easy for Ayesha to accept?
qa.a: Tenzin came with tea and named a specific task, handing out the bags at the sewing room the next day. He asked for nothing in return.

qa.q: What is it like for Ayesha when she says she is just tired and her voice cracks?
qa.a: Ayesha is exhausted and emotional, worn down by giving to everyone for so long. Letting someone else pour the tea is a relief after weeks of holding it in.

grounding: A tea-stall owner sees the village's usual giver become curt and withdrawn and offers help for a change.

passage: In their shared flat in Lisbon, Yuki was the one who remembered everyone's birthdays, fixed the Wi-Fi, and left soup outside doors when someone was sick. Gabriel had noticed the change over two weeks. Yuki stopped joining dinner. She answered questions with one word. On Thursday, when Gabriel asked where the spare key was, she said, "Figure it out yourself," and shut her door. Gabriel stood in the hallway, stung at first. Then he thought about her last month: two night shifts at the hotel, a sick friend, the move for her sister. He made rice and miso soup, badly, and knocked. "I'm not asking for anything," he said when she opened the door. "I just want to help you for once." Yuki stared at the tray, then her face crumpled. "I'm so tired," she whispered.

qa.q: What did Yuki say when Gabriel asked about the spare key?
qa.a: She said, 'Figure it out yourself,' and shut her door.

qa.q: What was Gabriel feeling in the hallway, and what changed?
qa.a: He felt stung at first, then his hurt turned to concern as he remembered how much Yuki had been carrying last month.

qa.q: What could Gabriel do after the soup?
qa.a: He could ask the other flatmates to take over some of Yuki's jobs, like the Wi-Fi and birthdays, and check in with her again in a few days.

qa.q: How might Yuki have felt when Gabriel brought the tray?
qa.a: She was probably relieved and moved that someone finally noticed her, which let her admit how tired she was.

grounding: Shows a flatmate noticing that the usual giver has become curt and withdrawn and offering to care for her for a change.

passage: In the staff room of Ward 6, Pallavi watched Jatin slam his locker. For two years he had been the nurse everyone called: swap my shift, cover my break, help me with the drip. Today he'd told a junior, "Can't you do anything yourself?" and walked off. Pallavi had never heard him say anything like that. She noticed his lunch box, untouched since morning, and the dark circles he'd been wearing for weeks. When he came back to fill his water bottle, she didn't lecture him. "Jatin, give me your two night shifts next week. I owe you about fifty." He frowned. "I'm fine." "You just shouted at Ruchi." He sat down heavily. "I haven't had a full day off in five weeks." Pallavi took out the roster and a pen right there.

qa.q: How long had it been since Jatin had a full day off?
qa.a: Five weeks.

qa.q: What was Pallavi thinking when she noticed Jatin's untouched lunch box?
qa.a: She seemed worried and concerned, reading his dark circles and snapping as signs he was worn out rather than just rude.

qa.q: How did Pallavi offer help in a way Jatin could accept?
qa.a: She skipped the lecture and made a specific offer, taking his night shifts, framed as paying back what she owed.

qa.q: What is it like for Jatin to be offered help after two years of helping?
qa.a: He resists at first, saying he is fine, then sits down heavily, which suggests he felt exhausted and relieved.

grounding: Shows a colleague noticing a usual giver becoming curt and withdrawn and stepping in to help him for once.

passage:
Dear Arnab,

I'm writing because every time I try to say this in person, you change the subject to someone else's problem.

You've been different these last few weeks. Short with the kids at the tuition centre. Leaving the group chat on "seen." Last Sunday you didn't come to cricket for the first time in three years. I know you've been driving your uncle to dialysis twice a week and covering the centre's accounts since Ravi left.

You're the one who always turns up for everyone. I don't think anyone has turned up for you.

So here's my offer. I'll take the Saturday batch for the next month. And on Wednesday I'm coming over with food, and you don't have to host. You can just eat.

Your friend,
Sudha

qa.q: How often has Arnab been driving an uncle to dialysis?
qa.a: Twice a week.

qa.q: What does Sudha seem to feel about the changes in Arnab?
qa.a: Sudha seems worried and caring, reading Arnab's curtness and absence as signs of being worn out rather than unfriendly.

qa.q: What small step does Sudha offer, and why is it well chosen?
qa.a: Taking the Saturday batch and bringing food with no hosting expected gives Arnab real rest without anything to manage.

qa.q: How might Arnab feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Arnab may feel exposed at first, then relieved and cared for, since no one has turned up for Arnab in a long time.

grounding: Shows a friend noticing that a usual giver has become curt and withdrawn and offering to help for a change.

passage: So there's this guy in my flat, Varun. I'm Swati, I've shared the flat with him and two others for three years, and Varun is the one who fixes everything. Wi-Fi, the landlord, someone's breakup, he's there. Last month I started noticing things. He stopped cooking on Sundays. He answered in one word. When Nikita asked him to look at her bike, he snapped, "Can someone else do it for once?" and went to his room. We all went quiet. My first thought was, rude. Then I thought, when did any of us last ask him anything? So I knocked. I said, "I'm doing your laundry this week and I'm making dinner on Sunday. Don't argue." He just stood in the doorway for a bit. Then he said, "Okay." That's it. Okay. But he ate two plates.

qa.q: What did Varun snap when Nikita asked about her bike?
qa.a: He snapped, "Can someone else do it for once?"

qa.q: What was Swati feeling after Varun snapped?
qa.a: Swati first felt annoyed and thought he was rude, then felt a guilty jolt, realising none of them had asked about Varun in a long time 😔

qa.q: What made Swati's offer work?
qa.a: It was concrete, laundry and Sunday dinner, and it didn't make Varun explain or ask, so he could simply accept.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Varun when Swati knocked?
qa.a: He was probably surprised and moved, since he stood in the doorway quietly before accepting, and being looked after was new for him.

grounding: Shows a flatmate noticing that the usual helper has turned curt and withdrawn, and offering to look after him for a change.
